title: Of all the creatures in the sea, LLMs seem to love cuttlefish the most
author: yenniejun111

excerpt: I built a virtual Aquarium and asked twelve different AI models to create an aquarium tank with one creature inside of it: “Your tank holds exactly one creature, and both the creature and its tank should be an expression of you: your personality, your sensibilities, what you find delightful.” I hoped these whimsical creatures could reveal something about each model’s creative tendencies. Of all the fish in the sea (!), the models seemed to converge on a few common sea creatures. In the screenshot above, you might notice there are two cuttlefish (created by two different Claude models) and two octopuses. This reminded me of a phenomenon called mode collapse, which is when a model produces repetitive outputs that lack diversity. I wanted to know how often these models gravitated toward the same creative ideas, so I decided to investigate. A mini-experiment: how different models display different creative habits To better understand how often particular animals and descriptors appeared, I asked each of the twelve models to imagine an underwater creature representing its personality, 50 times each (yielding 600 named creatures in total). Rather than having each model create an entire aquarium, I simplified the task to focus just on the creature names. In the prompt, each AI model was asked to describe its creature with adjectives using alliteration or onomatopoeia, which led to some fun monikers, such as “Sputtering Scribblefish,” “Pensive Puffling Pipfish,” and “Blooping Bellfish.” Some models kept returning to almost identical names, sometimes changing only a word or two. But there were plenty of wonderfully strange creations that appeared only once. For this analysis, I separated each creature type (e.g. cuttlefish, pufferfish) from its descriptors (e.g. spluttering, blubbering).
